 OPINION | India’s skilling ecosystem needs a local lens, not a national one 
 OPINION | India’s skilling ecosystem needs a local lens, not a national one 
 India has built considerable scale in skilling. The next step is to make sure that what people learn connects more closely with the work available to them. That is the last mile the skilling ecosystem must close 
 Gopal Devanahalli
 October 22, 2026 / 16:34 IST Share --> 
 --> 
 --> 
 --> 
 New skills 
 More than 7.67 crore people have been formally skilled in India since 2014-15, and key Central Ministries allocated around ₹34,000 crore for skilling-related expenditure in FY2025-26. Yet, the relevance of training still depends on a more immediate question: are institutions preparing people for the jobs employers need and learners can realistically access?    
 ITI network’s gaps 
 India’s ITI network makes the mismatch visible. Electrician and fitter trades continue to account for a disproportionate share of enrolment, even as employment opportunities span services, healthcare, logistics, digital work and the green economy. These traditional trades remain important, but they cannot be the only options available to learners as the economy changes.
 The gap becomes clearer when we look beyond national averages. NITI Aayog’s review points to vocational offerings that are often insufficiently connected to district-level economic demand and the employment opportunities available to students.
 Maharashtra’s district-level skill-gap assessments illustrate the range of requirements, from broadband technicians, CNC operators and industrial electricians to medical records assistants, emergency-care personnel and solar PV installers. Such differences affect what institutions teach, the practical training they provide and the employers they need to engage. Shorter, modular courses developed with employers and reviewed as demand changes could help institutions respond more quickly.

 Underutilised insights from placement data 
 Training institutions also have a source of intelligence that is often underused: their own placement experience.
 Every placement cycle raises questions worth examining. Which skills did employers find missing? What practical competencies, equipment or software did candidates need? Why did some hires fail to last the year? The answers can reveal where training falls short, provided institutions collect and use this information consistently.
 Too often, the outcome is reduced to a placement percentage. Recurring competency gaps could inform new modules, while persistently weak employment outcomes should prompt a review of the curriculum, delivery or relevance to available jobs. Placement reports should lead to decisions, not simply record results.
 That requires clearer institutional accountability. Training providers should be able to explain which gaps they identified, what they changed and whether those changes improved outcomes for subsequent batches. Without that follow-through, skill-gap assessments risk documenting problems without addressing them.
 It’s not national versus local 
 National standards remain essential to the quality and credibility of vocational training. Localisation should complement these standards, not replace them. Institutions need the flexibility to adapt course offerings and practical training to local employment opportunities, while ensuring learners gain recognised, transferable skills.
 This does not mean graduates must find work only in their own districts. They should be able to access suitable jobs nearby and pursue opportunities elsewhere when they choose or need to.
 Institutions and employers operating within the same ecosystem should compare what they are seeing at regular intervals. Findings from one hiring cycle should inform the next batch, rather than wait for a lengthy curriculum-revision process.
 This does not necessarily require another large national technology platform. A simple mechanism for nearby institutions and employers to exchange reliable information on vacancies, required skills, placements and retention would be a useful starting point.
 Enrolment and course completion show how many people entered and finished training. They do not establish whether that training led to suitable, sustainable employment. Placement, retention and wage progression therefore need more consistent tracking. National and state averages can conceal differences in employment opportunities and the need for graduates to migrate for work. These measures can also help distinguish between a temporary recruitment shortfall, a mismatch in training and a more fundamental lack of jobs.
 Industry participation must also extend beyond recruitment. Employers should help co-design modules, provide trainers, offer apprenticeships and give institutions structured feedback after each hiring cycle. Large employers can contribute scale and structured career pathways. Smaller firms can offer insight into changing skill requirements in their own markets.
 Much of this work need not wait for a new national scheme. State Skill Development Missions and District Skill Committees can bring institutions and employers together to identify common gaps and inform training priorities4. Institutions, however, must remain responsible for reviewing outcomes and acting on the evidence.
 The practical questions for every institution are straightforward: What are employers within reach of our graduates hiring for now? What prevented our students from securing or retaining those jobs? And what will we change before the next batch graduates?
 India has built considerable scale in skilling. The next step is to make sure that what people learn connects more closely with the work available to them, wherever they choose to pursue it. That is the last mile the skilling ecosystem must close.
 (Gopal Devanahalli, President, Skills Development Network.)
